weighted_score.interpretation: A net score of +0.1848 is a moderate bullish reading, roughly half the tactical score, and the gap is almost entirely explained by weight reallocation rather than by any change of stance: only Factor 3 flips direction and Factors 9 and 10 fall to Neutral. External Balance moves from 0.06 to 0.16 of weight, taking its contribution from -0.0318 to -0.0960, and Fiscal from 0.04 to 0.07, taking its contribution from -0.0208 to -0.0420. Those two alone remove 0.0854 from the score. Policy & Rates remains the dominant single contribution at +0.1392 and Guidance rises to +0.0696 on a heavier weight. The reading is therefore a directional view held with genuine humility: the cyclical case for the yen is strong and the structural case against it is also strong.
weighted_score.mapping_to_conviction: Using the same cycle-wide mapping -- below 0.05 is conviction 1, 0.05 to 0.15 is 2, 0.15 to 0.30 is 3, 0.30 to 0.45 is 4, above 0.45 is 5 -- a score of +0.1848 sits in the lower half of the band for conviction 3. We deliberately do not round up despite the score being comfortably positive, because the last twelve months provide direct evidence that the primary transmission mechanism for a strategic yen rally, ten-year spread compression, delivered 95bp of compression and a 4.92% yen DECLINE against the dollar.

strategic.rationale: At strategic weights the picture changes materially because External Balance rises from 0.06 to 0.16 and Guidance from 0.07 to 0.12, while Inflation & Growth halves from 0.18 to 0.10 and Flows falls from 0.10 to 0.06. Policy & Rates remains the largest single weight at 0.24 and remains Bullish at 58, because Japan is the only G10 economy whose policy rate sits unambiguously below its own central bank's neutral estimate -- 1.00% against a stated 'around 2 percent' -- while the Fed, the RBA and Norges Bank are all at or above neutral. The net score of +0.1848 is therefore a genuinely moderate reading rather than a strong one: the positive block of Policy & Rates at +0.1392, Guidance at +0.0696, Inflation & Growth at +0.0550, Flows at +0.0330 and Risk Appetite at +0.0260 totals +0.3228, and it is offset by -0.1380 from External Balance at -0.0960 and Fiscal at -0.0420. Those two negatives are the honest core of the bear case and they interact: Japan's terms of trade at 83.95 are 44% below their since-1960 average and its FY2026 debt-service assumption of 3.0% is a 29-year high, so the country is simultaneously paying more for energy and more for its own debt. The single most important observation in this dossier is a disconfirming one -- over the last twelve months the ten-year UST-JGB spread compressed roughly 95 basis points and the yen still fell 4.92% against the dollar and 13.14% against the Australian dollar, which means the traditional rate-differential channel stopped setting the price and a Japan-specific fiscal risk premium took over, visible in a 30-year JGB at 3.971% within 4bp of its all-time high. Any strategic yen-bullish case built purely on spread compression is therefore built on a broken correlation, and that is precisely why our strategic conviction is 3 rather than 4. What we expect that the market does not is a terminal Bank of Japan rate above 1.25%: OIS gives essentially no weight to anything higher within twelve months, while the board's own framework implies 100bp of latent tightening and a hawkish member is already voting for 1.25% today. The path of least resistance is a grinding, interrupted appreciation rather than a trend: we expect USD/JPY at 152.00 in six months against a six-month forward of 155.99, an edge of roughly 399 pips. The dated catalysts that carry the strategic view are the three remaining Bank of Japan meetings on 18 September, 30 October with a quarterly Outlook Report, and 18 December, plus the September Tankan on 1 October and the FY2027 budget and JGB issuance plan in late December. Conviction drivers are the valuation extreme, the policy-rate gap to neutral and a Ministry of Finance that has now spent roughly JPY 20 trillion establishing a credible ceiling; conviction detractors are the terms of trade, the fiscal trajectory and the GPIF rotation. Actionability is moderate: with the six-month forward already 2.53 yen below spot, a large part of the expected move is financed away by carry, so the strategic view is better expressed on the crosses -- short AUD/JPY, long JPY/CHF -- than in the primary pair.

g10_ranking.commentary: The yen ranks fourth of eleven strategically. It beats the dollar because the Fed is at or above neutral while the Bank of Japan is a full 100bp below its own, and it beats the low-yielding bloc of the Canadian dollar, franc, krona and Singapore dollar because none of them has a comparable policy-rate gap to close. It loses to the krone and the Australian dollar, both of which combine the highest policy rates in the set with favourable terms of trade in an energy-shock world, and to the euro, whose real effective exchange rate sits within 0.5% of its mean with a September hike close to fully priced and none of Japan's terms-of-trade or fiscal drag. The ranking would rise to second on a single condition: a 25bp hike on 18 September accompanied by guidance pointing at the board's 2% neutral rate.

If a hike is delivered, the second phase from October through December is a steady decline toward 154-155 supported by the 30 October Outlook Report and the December meeting, with the 155.00 level acting as the structural pivot -- a sustained monthly close below it confirms a lower high at 163.99 and ends the multi-year uptrend from the April 2025 low. consensus_divergence.consensus_view: The aggregated bank-forecast path has USD/JPY at 159.12 in September 2026, 157.82 in December 2026 and 156.10 in March 2027, implying the street expects the yen to recover only about 1.5% over six months and to remain far below its real effective mean indefinitely. The named dispersion is unusually wide: Goldman Sachs at 162 in three months, 163 in six and 165 in twelve, and J.P. Morgan at 164 for end-2026 anchor the yen-bearish camp on higher-for-longer US yields and Japanese fiscal concerns, while Citi and ING at 153, Scotiabank at 150, MUFG at 146 and Nomura at 140 anchor the bullish camp. Nomura's near-term tactical range was 162.00-165.50 as recently as 28 July. OIS prices only 21bp of Bank of Japan tightening through 18 December, and the September meeting is priced at 16-35% depending on which public representation is used.
consensus_divergence.our_view: We expect USD/JPY at 156.00 in one month, 154.00 in three and 152.00 in six, and we expect the Bank of Japan to deliver 50bp of tightening by end-Q1 2027 to 1.50% with a credible path toward the board's stated 2% neutral rate. That places us roughly 4 yen more yen-bullish than the aggregated consensus path at the six-month point and 11 to 13 yen more bullish than Goldman Sachs and J.P. Morgan, while remaining materially less bullish than MUFG at 146 and Nomura at 140.
consensus_divergence.divergence_magnitude: Approximately 400 pips, or 2.6%, versus the aggregated consensus path at six months (152.00 against roughly 156.10), and approximately 399 pips versus the six-month forward outright of 155.99. On the policy leg we are 25 to 50bp more hawkish on the Bank of Japan than OIS through Q1 2027.
consensus_divergence.why_we_differ: Three specific under-weightings. First, the guidance-versus-pricing gap: Governor Ueda said on 31 July that the Bank, if monetary conditions are accommodative, has 'a chance we could speed up the pace of interest rate hikes' and that it would debate policy 'from our next meeting onward', a board member is already voting for 1.25%, and the June Summary of Opinions places neutral 'at around 2 percent' -- yet public pricing for September is only 16-35% and just 21bp is priced cumulatively through December. Consensus is applying a historical credibility discount to a Bank of Japan that has already delivered 100bp of tightening. Second, the change in the official reaction function: two interventions in 2026 totalling roughly JPY 20 trillion, executed with a US Treasury report that describes 'substantial yen undervaluation' and endorses normalisation, means the ceiling above 160 is more credible than it has been at any point since 2022, and consensus is still extrapolating the 2024 template in which intervention failed. Third, positioning: a combined leveraged and asset-manager net short of 176,091 contracts, beyond the historical extreme threshold and still building into the high, is a mechanical source of yen demand that forecast models do not capture. Consensus over-weights the carry level, which is already fully expressed in a six-month forward 253 pips below spot and therefore cannot be an edge.
consensus_divergence.payoff_if_right: A move to 152.00 at six months delivers 652 pips, of which 399 pips is edge over the forward, and 792 pips on a short AUD/JPY expression if half the 14.2% valuation gap between 111.52 spot and 95.68 relative-REER fair value closes. Positions taken through options rather than spot pay off disproportionately because one-month implied volatility below 6.0 against twenty-day realised of 9.58% means the convexity is being sold too cheaply.
consensus_divergence.risk_if_wrong: If Goldman Sachs and J.P. Morgan are right and USD/JPY is at 163-165 in six months, a long-yen position loses 450 to 650 pips plus roughly 253 pips of carry over the period, a total drawdown of 4.4% to 5.7%. The specific mechanism by which we would be wrong is the one we identify in Factor 8: higher Japanese yields continuing to reflect fiscal risk rather than policy tightening, which delivers a steeper curve, a weaker currency and no relief.

cleanest_bullish_expression.rationale: The single cleanest expression of a bullish-yen view. It combines the widest policy-rate differential in the set at 335bp, which makes it the most crowded carry leg and therefore the most convex to an unwind; the widest valuation gap at 14.2%, with the yen 7.82% below its own real effective mean and the Australian dollar 6.42% above its own after a 9.81% year-on-year real appreciation; and the highest risk beta in G10 FX, since AUD/JPY is the purest risk barometer available. The cross has gained 13.14% on the yen over twelve months and sits 17.64% above its twelve-month low of 94.80, against a twelve-month high of 114.84, so the accumulated carry position is at its most vulnerable. The carry cost of 335bp is the price of admission and it is real, but the risk-adjusted cost at -0.35 carry-to-vol is actually less punitive than USD/JPY at -0.41 because the cross carries more volatility.

cleanest_bearish_expression.rationale: If the yen-bullish thesis fails, the cleanest short-yen expression is against the krone. Norges Bank runs the highest policy rate in the G10 at 4.25%, has guided explicitly that 'the policy rate will be raised at one of the forthcoming meetings' with a live decision on 13 August, and Norway is the direct beneficiary of the same energy shock that has driven Japan's mineral fuel imports up 41.9% year-on-year and its terms of trade down 5.0% in a single month. That is a genuine double positive rather than a simple carry trade: the 325bp differential is paid for by an oil-driven current account surplus of 15.59% of GDP against Japan's deteriorating goods balance. The cross has gained 12.72% on the yen over twelve months and was one of only two pairs in the set in which the yen LOST ground during the intervention month, falling 1.81% against the krone and 1.12% against the New Zealand dollar while gaining against everything else.

relative_value_pairs.thesis: The only relationship in the benchmarking set in which the yen earns positive carry -- 100bp today, 125bp after one Bank of Japan hike and 150bp after two, against a Swiss National Bank pinned at 0.00% by 0.5% inflation and expected to hold throughout 2026. The yen is additionally 7.7% cheap to the franc on relative real effective deviation, and the ten-year JGB yields 234bp more than the Swiss Confederation bond. This is a positive-carry, positive-valuation, safe-haven-versus-safe-haven position that also performs in a risk-off scenario, which makes it the highest-quality relative-value structure available on the yen and one that does not require the directional thesis to be right.

A quieter relative-value trade with an unusual feature: Japan is one of only two sovereigns in the set that out-yields Singapore at ten years, with the JGB at 2.801% against the SGS at 2.36%, a 44bp advantage, while the Monetary Authority of Singapore runs no policy rate and has only tightened the S$NEER slope 'very slightly'. The yen is 7.7% cheap to the Singapore dollar on relative real effective deviation despite the yield advantage, and the cross has gained 6.06% on the yen over twelve months purely through band mechanics rather than any rate differential.

The purest test of relative monetary trajectories in the set. The Bank of Canada has held six consecutive times at 2.25% with CPI-trim at 1.8% and CPI-median at 1.9%, both BELOW the 2% midpoint, and the Canadian economy contracted 0.05% year-on-year; the Bank of Japan has hiked to 1.00% with corporate inflation expectations rising at every horizon. The 125bp gap is the one most likely to close from the peer leg, and at 79bp the ten-year yield give-up is the smallest Japan faces in the G10 dollar bloc.

cross_horizon_consistency.summary: Both horizons are net Bullish for the yen -- tactical +0.3606 with conviction 4, strategic +0.1848 with conviction 3 -- so the direction is aligned and the divergence is entirely in magnitude and confidence.
cross_horizon_consistency.divergence_explanation: The conviction gap is mechanical rather than analytical. Only one factor changes direction between horizons (Risk Appetite, Neutral to Bullish) and two fall to Neutral (Market Structure and USD Liquidity); every other stance is identical. The score halves because the weights reallocate: External Balance rises from 0.06 to 0.16, taking its contribution from -0.0318 to -0.0960, and Fiscal from 0.04 to 0.07, taking its contribution from -0.0208 to -0.0420, while Inflation & Growth halves from 0.18 to 0.10 and Flows falls from 0.10 to 0.06. In other words the tactical case rests on catalysts, positioning and data surprises that carry heavy short-horizon weight, while the strategic case has to survive the terms of trade and the fiscal trajectory, which carry heavy long-horizon weight and are both negative.
cross_horizon_consistency.inflection_point: The 18 September Bank of Japan meeting, with the 30 October meeting and its quarterly Outlook Report as the confirming event. Structurally the inflection level is 155.00: a sustained monthly close below it confirms a lower high at 163.99 and ends the multi-year uptrend from the April 2025 low, at which point the tactical and strategic cases converge.
cross_horizon_consistency.catalyst_for_transition: A 25bp hike to 1.25% accompanied by guidance pointing at the board's 2% neutral rate would raise the strategic conviction from 3 to 4 and re-rank the yen from fourth to second in the G10 plus SGD set. Conversely, holds at both the September and October meetings would cut strategic conviction to 2 and leave the tactical case as a completed squeeze with nothing behind it.
cross_horizon_consistency.trading_implication: Size the tactical view larger than the strategic view and express it through options while one-month implied volatility is below realised; express the strategic view through the crosses -- short AUD/JPY and long JPY/CHF -- where the valuation gap is widest and the carry cost is either offset by convexity or actually positive, rather than in USD/JPY where the six-month forward already finances away 39% of the expected move.

factors_changed.reason: The policy rate is unchanged at 1.00% but the guidance around it has moved decisively. On 1 July the Bank had just hiked and was assumed to pause; on 31 July it held 8-1 with Takata dissenting for 1.25% and Ueda said the Bank 'could speed up the pace of interest rate hikes'. Tactically that converts a factor generating no signal into one with a measurable guidance-versus-pricing gap of roughly 15-20 percentage points on September. Strategic confidence is trimmed from 64 to 58 because a further month of evidence showed the ten-year spread compressing without the yen benefiting.

Three hawkish data points arrived that the July report could not have seen: Tokyo July core at 1.9% against a 1.7% consensus with core-core at 2.0%, June domestic corporate goods prices at +7.1% year-on-year with yen-based import prices at +29.7%, and a July Outlook Report that raised FY2027 core CPI to 2.4% while attributing the FY2026 cut purely to energy subsidies. The June Tankan also beat at +22 for large manufacturers with corporate inflation expectations rising at all three horizons.

The risk environment is no less benign -- equities at records, high-yield spreads at 287bp -- but the compression has become extreme enough on three separate volatility tenors simultaneously that it now reads as a contrarian condition rather than a simple headwind. The 30 July session demonstrated the mechanism live: a 3% yen move on a day when the VIX did not spike, which is positioning, not risk aversion.

The short grew rather than covering. The July report cited roughly -146,000 contracts of net non-commercial positioning; the 21 July report shows combined leveraged and asset-manager net short of 176,091, with asset managers alone adding 26,089 contracts in a single week. The squeeze catalyst then fired on 30 July, which is why tactical confidence rises from 61 to 65 -- the highest reading in this dossier. The 28 July report, published before the valuation date, shows the short growing further to a combined 185,047.

The single largest stance reversal of the month, and it is entirely energy. The July report was written with Brent near USD 73; Brent then spiked to USD 105.32 on 23 July before settling at USD 91.82. June mineral fuel imports rose 41.9% year-on-year, the trade balance posted a second consecutive deficit at JPY 406.9bn against a JPY 120bn consensus, and terms of trade fell 5.0% in a single month to 83.95. This reversal alone removes roughly 0.20 from the strategic score.

Direction unchanged; tactical confidence still falls slightly from 58 to 58 on an unchanged reading after verification lowered it from 62, because the guidance-versus-pricing gap rests partly on OIS representations that conflict, while strategic confidence falls from 64 to 58 because the Bank held when it could have hiked into a 40-year low, and because the Takaichi political constraint became more visible through the June Summary of Opinions.

The July report treated geopolitical escalation as net yen-positive. A further month of evidence contradicted that: the Hormuz escalation of mid-July drove Brent above USD 100 and the yen WEAKENED to a 40-year low, demonstrating that for Japan the energy channel now offsets the safe-haven channel. Downgraded to Neutral on both horizons.

Upgraded from background to material. The 30-year JGB set an all-time high of 4.013% on 9 July and closed 30 July at 3.971%, the government revised its FY2026 debt estimate up to 187.6% of GDP, and the FY2026 budget's 3.0% debt-service assumption is a 29-year high. Critically, this is the identified mechanism by which higher Japanese yields have coincided with a weaker yen.

Direction unchanged but the content is entirely new: spot has broken below the 50-day at 161.369 and the 100-day at 160.083 while remaining 55 pips above the 200-day at 157.975, and twenty-day realised volatility nearly doubled from 5.11% to 9.58% while one-month implied sat below 6.0. Tactical confidence was lowered from 58 to 52 after verification showed the moving-average break is partial rather than complete.

Tactically upgraded on the dollar leg rather than the funding leg: US Q2 GDP slowed to +1.5% annualised from +2.1% and June headline PCE fell 0.1% on the month, undercutting the three FOMC hike dissenters within a day of the vote. Strategic remains Neutral with confidence trimmed to 50 because the JPY/USD cross-currency basis remained unobtainable for a second consecutive cycle.

seasonality.pattern: Three documented seasonal patterns bear on the yen inside the horizons. First and largest, the Japanese fiscal year-end on 31 March generates well-documented repatriation flows from late February through March as Japanese corporates and institutions bring foreign earnings home for accounting purposes -- a reliably yen-positive window. Second, the 31 December year-end dollar funding turn reliably widens cross-currency basis and creates a temporary dollar bid against the yen, a predictable yen headwind concentrated in the final two weeks of December. Third, and specific to this cycle, the Japanese government's summer energy subsidy programme -- explicitly named by the Bank of Japan as the reason FY2026 core CPI was cut from 2.8% to 2.5% -- rolls off during the strategic window, which mechanically lifts measured core inflation into FY2027 independent of any change in underlying price pressure.
seasonality.relevance_window: The December funding turn and the energy-subsidy roll-off both fall inside the one-to-six-month strategic window, which runs to approximately 1 February 2027. The March fiscal-year-end repatriation flow falls just OUTSIDE it, though the market typically begins anticipating it from late January, so it is a supportive influence at the very end of the window rather than a driver within it. Nothing seasonal falls inside the two-to-four-week tactical window, which is one reason seasonality is not part of the tactical case.
seasonality.historical_magnitude: Not quantified this cycle. We could not retrieve a citable historical distribution of yen returns around the December funding turn or the March fiscal year-end, and we decline to assert a magnitude we have not measured. The directional logic is well documented and the dates are certain; the size is not established and this is flagged as a gap. The one magnitude we can state is policy-derived rather than statistical: the Bank of Japan attributed a 30 basis point cut to its FY2026 core CPI forecast to the energy subsidies, which implies a comparable mechanical uplift as they expire.
seasonality.current_alignment: Net seasonal skew over the strategic window is mildly yen-positive but back-loaded. The December funding turn is the one predictable moment at which the yen faces a headwind and it argues for expecting the counter-rally we describe in the strategic path expectation. The energy-subsidy roll-off reinforces the Bullish stance on Factor 2 and the hawkish reading of the July Outlook Report. The anticipation of March repatriation supports the final leg toward our 152.00 target in late January. None of this is load-bearing for either stance.

The 1M -41.35, 3M -124.84, 6M -253.38 and 12M -494.80 pip figures come from a dated vendor snapshot taken at 22:03 UTC on 23 July 2026 with a spot reference of 163.832, and have been rebased to the 158.52 close on the assumption that forward points are approximately invariant to a five-yen spot move. An independent onshore FX-swap source dated 9 June corroborates the shape (1M -40.80, 3M -116.47, 6M -232.89). All forward outrights and all edge calculations inherit this approximation.

Implied volatility levels are PARTIAL. No full 1W/1M/3M/6M/1Y USD/JPY ATM strip for 28-31 July 2026 was obtainable from any public source. The 1M figure of 6.0 is taken from a report describing 1M ATM falling below 6.0 in the week to 24 July, and the 3M figure of 6.4 from a published USD/JPY implied-volatility index reading of 6.36 on 28 July. The one-year IV percentile of 8 is INFERRED from published five-year REALISED percentiles (1M 0.5th, 3M 10th, 6M 9.2nd) plus the sub-6.0 ATM print, not measured. All carry-to-vol ratios in Factor 1 use estimated cross-pair 3M implied volatilities and are labelled as estimates. These figures almost certainly repriced higher after 30 July.

The three-month JPY/USD, EUR/USD and GBP/USD cross-currency basis levels were NOT OBTAINABLE from any public source this cycle. The currency brief identifies the JPY/USD basis as a critical monitor for Factor 10, so its absence is a material gap and is the explicit reason Factor 10 confidence is capped at 52 tactical and 50 strategic. No basis figure has been estimated or asserted.

The JPY 8.45 trillion size of the 30 July intervention is a Bloomberg ESTIMATE derived from Bank of Japan current-account projections, not an official figure. The Ministry of Finance's disclosure covering the 30 July to 27 August window will not be published until late August. The only officially confirmed 2026 intervention is JPY 11,734.9bn for the 28 April to 27 May window. Every reference to the 30 July size in this dossier carries that qualification.

The BIS real broad effective exchange rate percentile of 3 for the yen, and every PPP deviation in the valuation table, are computed from a 30-observation monthly cached series covering January 2024 to June 2026. This window cannot support a decade-length distribution. Deviations are calculated as the difference between each currency's percentage deviation from its own 30-month mean, so they measure relative real-effective cheapness rather than absolute purchasing-power parity, and should be read as ordinal rather than as precise fair values.

Singapore has no policy interest rate; the Monetary Authority of Singapore manages the S$NEER within an undisclosed band. The policy_rate field for SGD is therefore null in both reference tables, and where a short-rate comparison is required the two-year SGS yield of 1.92% as at 27 July is used as an explicit proxy.

Japan CPI is sourced from the Statistics Bureau of Japan and reputable secondary reporting rather than from the OECD cache, because the OECD series for Japan is frozen at 2021. Euro-area GDP and unemployment and all Singapore macro data are likewise web-sourced, and every central bank's preferred core measure and all non-US policy rates come from central bank publications or dated market reporting rather than from the cache.

The prior compatible dossier used for the Change Since Last Report section was read from the engine dossiers folder rather than from the repository cycle folder at Analysis/2026-07-01/Base/, which was empty at the time of this run. The file is the same v2.0 JPY dossier dated 2026-07-01.

Moving averages and realised volatility are computed on a WEEKDAY-ONLY basis (50, 100 and 200 trading observations; 20-, 5- and 60-observation realised windows annualised at sqrt(252)). The cached Twelve Data FX series contains some weekend fills, and computing on the raw series inflates the 200-day moving average to 158.88 and produces a spurious full moving-average break. The corrected 200-day is 157.975, spot is above it, and the trend break is therefore PARTIAL. Performance windows are calendar-anchored to 30 June, 30 April, 30 January and 31 July 2025 rather than fixed observation counts, for the same reason.

This dossier was subjected to an adversarial verification pass before publication. Twenty-five headline items were confirmed against primary sources including every arithmetic check; fourteen were flagged and every one has been corrected or annotated inline; eight remain unverifiable and are labelled as such. Six factor confidences were LOWERED as a direct result -- Policy & Rates tactical 55 to 50, Flows tactical 68 to 65, External Balance tactical 55 to 53 and strategic 62 to 60, Guidance tactical 62 to 58, Fiscal tactical 55 to 52 and strategic 62 to 60, and Market Structure tactical 58 to 52 -- taking the tactical weighted score from +0.3790 to +0.3606 and the strategic from +0.1850 to +0.1848 without any stance changing.

Public sources for Bank of Japan rate pricing CONFLICT and neither has been suppressed. A TONA-futures aggregator shows roughly 30% for 18 September, 60% for 30 October and 81% for 18 December; an OIS-implied rate ladder of 1.04%, 1.11% and 1.21% for the same meetings implies roughly 16%, 44% and 84%. The two agree only on the 21bp cumulative figure through December. We report the 16-35% range for September, and the conflict is the explicit reason Factor 1 tactical confidence is 50 and Factor 6 tactical confidence is 58.

Several figures reported by the research process could not be corroborated and are excluded or flagged rather than used: the June 2026 US core PCE reading (sources give both 3.3% and 2.8%), Japan's sovereign CDS spread (no public level obtainable), the exact 25-delta risk-reversal magnitudes for late July, the Japan ten-year breakeven inflation rate, and the Citi Economic Surprise Index for Japan.
